name: TensorRT-LLM
notable_features: PyExecutor background loop with a Scheduler, KVCacheManager, ModelEngine and Sampler; requests are fetched, scheduled, KV-allocated, then run
Overlap Scheduler is on by default: it launches GPU work for step n+1 while the CPU processes step n, at the cost of one extra decoding step of pipeline depth
CUDA Graph capture with padding up to the nearest captured batch size, documented as worth up to 22% end-to-end throughput on some models
Full parallelism menu: TP, PP, DP, EP, CP and Wide-EP with an expert-parallel load balancer for MoE
Disaggregated prefill/decode serving and day-0 support cadence for new open-weight models
Also hosts a diffusion VisualGen pipeline for image/video generation

Engine build time is a tracked internal KPI: an open NVIDIA issue (2026-02-17) asks to display per-model engine build time, regressions and the slowest build in an internal dashboard - so the vendor treats this cost as something to optimise, not absorb

FMHA generation kernels are NVRTC-compiled at engine startup and the project is actively working to overlap that with autotuning and CUDA-graph capture (opt-in TRTLLM_GEN_FMHA_ASYNC_WARMUP=1, PR open as of 2026-10-04)
hardware_caveats: CUDA only - there is no ROCm, Metal, Vulkan or CPU path. This is the defining constraint of the engine

Version pinning is severe: the pip wheel is built against a specific PyTorch and CUDA Toolkit (docs show CUDA Toolkit 13.1 and a pinned torch cu130 wheel), and a documented failure mode is pip replacing your CUDA-13-compatible torch with a CUDA 12.8 build, leaving an unusable install until you lock torch with a constraints file
The wheel is not interchangeable with the NGC container's torch; inside an NGC PyTorch container you must use the prebuilt wheel shipped at /app/tensorrt_llm instead of the PyPI one
Slurm clusters need MPI rebuilt with Slurm support or the launcher aborts; this is called out as a general MPI+Slurm issue but it bites in practice

DeepGEMM expert-parallel kernels hard-abort after a 60s barrier budget (DG_JIT_BARRIER_TIMEOUT_SECONDS) and the resulting device-side assert poisons the CUDA context, so the first Python traceback points at an unrelated kernel
MoE scaling features (Wide-EP, EPLB, one-sided all-to-all over NVLink, DWDP) are written against NVLink topologies such as NVL72, so their published wins do not transfer to PCIe-only boxes

TWO SEPARATE BUILD COSTS, and the second one is on the startup path. (1) The C++ compile: NVIDIA's own CUDA-12 CI leg cost MORE THAN 5 HOURS on SBSA/Grace Blackwell and was DELETED to save the time rather than optimised (PR #7633, 2025-09-09) - a vendor self-report of NVIDIA's own build cost and the most direct published figure for this engine. (2) The runtime engine build for one checkpoint: 2+ hours observed for a DeepSeek-R1 build stage on a B200 following the official quick-start recipe (issue #8286, TensorRT-LLM 1.0.0.rc6, CUDA 12.8, driver 570.133.20), and a measured 290 s -> 260 s for Nemotron Super V3 fp8 at TP=8 (PR #11250). Separately, FMHA kernel NVRTC codegen costs '~5-11s per kernel variant depending on host CPU, 80-160s total on MLA fp8-KV configs (DeepSeek-family), ~2min for sparse gen kernels' on EVERY engine cold start (PR #18542). See [[ev-build-cost-is-three-separate-builds]]

The build guide's own dependency list is the real constraint: git-lfs checkout of large model assets, a purpose-built NGC devel container rather than a generic PyTorch image, mandatory Docker flags with stated failure modes ('--ipc=host is required to avoid Bus error (core dumped)'), a build-script-created virtualenv, and Conan for C++ dependencies. Network filesystems (Lustre/NFS/GPFS) are documented as much slower than local disk because a full build creates a very large number of small files
best_for: Maximum throughput on a fixed NVIDIA fleet, especially MoE models where expert parallelism and load balancing are the bottleneck
Deployments that can afford a build-time/version-lock step in exchange for hand-tuned kernels, CUDA graphs and the overlap scheduler
Latency-bound single-request serving on datacenter NVIDIA parts
avoid_for: Environments where you cannot control the CUDA and PyTorch versions, or where an unexpected pip resolution would be unrecoverable
Teams that need to support many model architectures without NVIDIA adding support for each
notes: 'paged-kv' and 'in-flight batching' both apply: the KVCacheManager allocates blocks and requests are added to a running batch rather than waiting for it to drain. Format support is recorded conservatively - the engine's own quantization path plus Model Optimizer checkpoints (FP8/FP4) are the well-trodden ones. Whether Marlin kernels are selectable inside TRT-LLM was not confirmed from the pages read, so treat that entry as uncertain. ||| MAINTENANCE (dated fact, GitHub API, 2026-10-04): last commit 2026-10-04 (0 months), latest release v1.2.1 published 2026-04-20, 493 contributors, open_issues_count 1571 (issues PLUS pull requests), NOT archived, 14762 stars. Actively developed, with a ~6-month gap between the latest release and the last commit - worth knowing if you are pinning to a release rather than tracking main. The docs site is currently serving 1.3.0rc29, i.e. AHEAD of the shipped v1.2.1 tag, so any capability read from the live docs is release-candidate behaviour rather than released behaviour. DEPLOYMENT: NO graded evidence of production deployment found - see [[ev-production-evidence-is-scarce-and-nearly-always-single-site]]. NVIDIA ships TensorRT-LLM inside NIM microservices, which is real commercial distribution, but NVIDIA publishes no request volume, QPS or fleet size for it and no independent third-party benchmark of the engine as deployed was found. The existing vendor-reported performance records for this engine remain the only throughput figures in the repo, and they are marked as such. PERFORMANCE CHARACTERISTICS: this engine has the repo's second-deepest set of vendor benchmarks (23 records) and they are unusually well-conditioned - engine version, model, quantization, TP degree and batch all stated - so this is one of the two engines in the repo where a reader can actually compare numbers. STRUCTURED OUTPUT and CHUNKED PREFILL: neither is recorded for this engine and neither was confirmed from the pages read on 2026-10-04 - recorded as UNSTATED rather than absent. MARLIN RESOLUTION: the record's own note flagged its marlin entry as uncertain; the 2026-10-04 read of the quantization docs did NOT resolve it. The versioned page's quick-links point instead at KV Cache Compression and at NVIDIA Model Optimizer's external support matrix, i.e. the vendor's own pointer for which quantizations work is ModelOpt's matrix, not this engine's docs - so the conservative supported_formats list stands unchanged and the marlin entry remains unconfirmed rather than being upgraded on the strength of a page that does not address it.
